title: Average-case RSA inversion versus factoring for exponent 65537
formal: For the fixed exponent \(e=65537\) and the balanced-prime ensemble below, does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time RSA inverter with inverse-polynomial average success imply the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm with inverse-polynomial average success?
definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 3\) let \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) be the finite set of primes p with \(2^{n- 1}\le p<2^{n}\) and \(\gcd (e,p- 1)=1\). Choose an ordered pair \((p,q)\) uniformly from \(\{(p,q)\in \mathrm{P}_{n}^{2}:p\ne q\}\), and set \(N=pq\). All assertions are for sufficiently large n with at least two such primes. Conditional on N, choose x uniformly from \(Z_{N}^{*}=\{a\in \{0,\ldots ,N- 1\}:\gcd (a,N)=1\}\), independently of algorithm coins, and set \(y=x^{e}\) mod N. The inverter I receives \((1^{n},N,y)\), in binary except for \(1^{n}\), and must output the unique \(x\in Z_{N}\)^* with that image. Nonnegligible success here means that some integer \(a\ge 1\) and \(n_{0}\) exist such that \(\Pr [I(1^{n},N,y)=x]\ge n^{- a}\) for every \(n\ge n_{0}\). The factoring algorithm F receives \((1^{n},N)\) and succeeds by outputting p or q; require some \(b\ge 1\) and \(n_{1}\) such that \(\Pr [F(1^{n},N)\in \{p,q\}]\ge n^{- b}\) for every \(n\ge n_{1}\). Both machines use independent fair random bits and have worst-case running time bounded by their own fixed polynomials in their input lengths on every random tape. The probabilities average over the stated modulus ensemble as well as x and the coins, with no promise of success separately on each modulus. The assertion is the ordinary existence implication \((\exists I,a,n_{0})\Rightarrow (\exists F,b,n_{1})\). It does not restrict a proof to black-box reductions: a construction of F may use the fixed code of I and count all calls to it in F’s polynomial running time. No independent oracle or advice is supplied.

context_blocks.text: Factoring an RSA modulus gives the private exponent and hence breaks encryption, but the reverse reduction is a longstanding cryptographic question. It would identify whether RSA inversion rests on precisely the factoring assumption or on a potentially weaker computational task.

Boneh’s survey asks about factoring with an RSA inversion oracle. This card retains the imported fixed-exponent average-case specialization and explicitly compares inverse-polynomial average success on its balanced-prime ensemble. The implication permits arbitrary constructions; restricted-model separation results do not refute it.

why: Identify the computational assumption underlying one of the central public-key primitives.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the stated existence implication for this exact ensemble and success convention. A refutation must establish that the inverter existence premise can hold while the factoring conclusion fails; merely ruling out a selected black-box reduction does not refute the implication. Results for special keys, different exponents, or worst-case inversion must be related to this average-case target before they count.
